lesson_title: The Thermometer That Refuses to Move
hook_text: Your stove is on FULL. The water is boiling. So why is the thermometer completely stuck?
clip_script: Put a pot of water on the stove with a thermometer in it. The temperature climbs steadily — forty, sixty, eighty, ninety-nine, one hundred. Then it stops. The plate is still glowing, the electricity is still costing somebody money, and the reading refuses to pass one hundred until the pot has nearly boiled dry. Where is all that energy going? Not into making the particles faster. Temperature only measures how hard the particles jiggle on average — so if the thermometer is stuck, the jiggling is not increasing. The energy is doing a different job: prising the particles apart. Water particles grip one another, and turning liquid into steam means breaking every one of those grips. Think of it as paying off a debt before you can save. Every joule goes straight to the debt collector — the forces holding the particles together — and only once the debt is settled does the balance climb again. The same trick happens at zero, while ice melts. And here is the sting in the tail: steam pays that whole debt BACK when it condenses — straight into your skin. That is why a steam burn is so much worse than boiling water. One stuck thermometer, and you now understand every flat line on every heating curve.
visual_style: Macro pot-side shot with an oversized analogue thermometer needle trembling at one hundred; cutaway to glowing particles straining against elastic bonds that snap one by one; a ledger animation stamping joules against a debt column until it zeroes and the needle finally sweeps up.
mood: Kitchen mystery with a physics payoff — ordinary appliance, stubborn little needle, satisfying explanation.
pacing: Countdown build to the stall, puzzled beat, debt-collector reveal, steam-burn sting, clean closing line.
